summary: Redwood AE + SE ran a 42-minute demo for Novara Retail showing the Conversations/Generations API quickstart, streaming behavior, parameter effects (temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop), and retry/backoff patterns. Discussed hosted vs dedicated tradeoffs for latency/cost, VPC options, SOC 2/KMS questions, and next steps for a short pilot and benchmarks.
transcript:
00:00:02 Maya (Redwood - AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We wanted to run through a short Conversations API quickstart and show streaming behavior, how params affect output, and the recommended retry/backoff patterns. Is this still the right agenda?
00:00:14 Carla (Novara): Yep, that's perfect. We're mainly worried about latency for live chat on our checkout flow and cost. Also Lina wanted to confirm security posture and VPC options.
00:00:26 Maya: Great. Aaron will lead most of the technical demo. Aaron?
00:00:31 Aaron (Redwood - SE): Hey all. Quick note, I'll demo from the Console and then jump to a small script to show streaming and retries. There may be a couple of mis-transcripts on my end, sorry in advance.
00:00:45 Aaron: (screen share sound) First, navigate to Console -> Models -> Conversations. You can see our recommended open models and redwood-verified perf numbers. For this demo I'm using rwd-neo-7b-quant as a low-latency variant.
00:01:06 Ethan (Novara): Quick Q: that model name, is that hosted-only or can we use equivalent on Dedicated?
00:01:12 Aaron: Good question. You can pin the same model family across Hosted and Dedicated — the runtime picks quantization and kernels per infra. So yes you can run a variant on Dedicated; latency characteristics will differ by GPU class.
00:01:29 Aaron: Now a simple streaming example; we call /v1/conversations.generate?stream=true and you get partial token frames. Here's a sample: we set temperature=0.2, max_tokens=150, stop=["\nUser:"] and we stream.
00:01:50 (15s) Aaron: [demo typing] You'll notice the first frame is quick with prefix tokens, then tokens stream as the model composes. This is useful to show typing UX immediately.
00:02:10 Lina (Novara): Are those frames guaranteed order? What about dropped frames if the client disconnects?
00:02:18 Aaron: Frames are delivered in order, but network issues can cause incomplete finalization. We recommend clients ack receipt and re-request partial context if needed, or rely on final non-streamed call for idempotent tasks. For chat you can resume via the convo id.
00:02:35 Maya: Important to note retries — we generally advise exponential backoff with jitter, and an overall idempotency policy for restarts.
00:02:46 Carla: Can you show how params like temperature and top_p change outputs? We have some hallucination concerns in product descriptions.
00:02:52 Aaron: Yep. Quick demo: same prompt, temp=0.0 -> output is deterministic and factual-leaning, but can be terse. temp=0.8 and top_p=0.9 -> more creative and risk of hallucination increases. We showed a before/after slide (link: https://redwood.ai/decks/conv-api-quickstart).
00:03:20 (30s) Aaron: Also max_tokens caps response length which can reduce hallucinations by constraining output. Stop sequences help to prevent accidental run-on. For structured outputs we prefer using function-calling or schema enforcement in the prompt.
00:03:45 Ethan: For throughput, how do you recommend batching vs low latency? Our checkout chat must respond sub-300ms for quick suggestions.
00:03:55 Aaron: If sub-300ms P95 is required, we typically recommend Dedicated on an A100 or H100 class with optimized model quantization and pinned runtime. Hosted can hit low latency too but cost may scale. Also auto prefix/KV cache can drop repeated prefixes significantly.
00:04:12 Aaron: On the API side, use smaller sequence sizes, set max_tokens conservatively, and enable prefix cache when you have repeated system/user patterns.
00:04:25 Lina: You mentioned cache — is that something we manage? Does it store customer data persistently?
00:04:33 Aaron: Cache is handled by Redwood runtime; you can opt-out or configure TTL. For Private/VPC deployments you can select no persistent cache or local-only; we have KMS integrations so cached KV is encrypted at rest.
00:04:50 (10s) {crosstalk}
00:05:05 Maya: Security checklist — they asked about SOC 2, SAML SSO, audit logs and KMS. We have SOC 2 Type II docs and SAML/SCIM support for enterprise, plus audit logs in the Console. I'll share the security pack.
00:05:22 Carla: Great. For the pilot we're thinking of sending a sample prompt set that includes PII, can you confirm data retention for hosted?
00:05:30 Aaron: Hosted offers configurable retention and deletion policies, and we offer Private deployments for no-data-leaving-the-premises requirements. For hosted we can enable auto-delete and restrict retention to 30/90/365 days per agreement. We'll include the specifics in the security pack.
00:05:48 (30s) Aaron: Now retry/backoff patterns: typical guidance — 5xx or rate limit (429) triggers exponential backoff: initial wait ~200-500ms, multiply by 2 with jitter, cap at 5-10s, and give up after N attempts (e.g., 4). For streaming, if the connection drops mid-stream, re-request with the last received token index and let the server resume.
00:06:15 Ethan: Does the SDK handle resume transparently?
00:06:20 Aaron: Our SDKs have helpers for streaming resumes and recommended retry policies, but for complex flows we suggest a lightweight wrapper to implement idempotency and application-level dedupe.
00:06:33 Maya: Quick note on cost: console shows cost breakdown by model and token type — input vs output tokens. We'll show that chart now.
00:06:44 Aaron: (screen share) Here are per-token unit economics. You can tune to cheaper variants or quantization levels for the same model family. Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization + batch settings based on your workload sample.
00:07:05 Carla: Can Optimize suggest batching without hurting latency SLOs?
00:07:10 Aaron: Yes — it analyzes request shapes and gives a plan: small batching windows for high-concurrency paths, and per-route settings. We can simulate with your traces.
00:07:25 (20s) Aaron: Now I'll break out to a small node script showing streaming with retries. (reads) const res = await client.conversations.generate({stream: true, model: 'rwd-neo-7b-quant', temperature:0.2, max_tokens:120, stop:['\nUser:']}); res.on('data', frame => { /* append UI */}); If a 429 is received, we backoff and re-try with lastMessageId.
00:08:05 Ethan: That lastMessageId, is it a RW conversation id?
00:08:10 Aaron: Yes, the convo id is returned and you can resume. For POCs we often store server-side conversation state so the client can reconstruct quickly.
00:08:24 (15s) Aaron: Note: network reordering and partial frames are possible; clients should be tolerant of duplicated tokens. We also emit deterministic frame ids to help dedupe.
00:08:45 Lina: Any particular pitfalls you've seen in production?
00:08:50 Aaron: Biggest ones — not constraining max_tokens, not using stop seq for structured outputs, and naive retry loops that duplicate charges. Also using zero-backoff on 429 which floods the server.
00:09:06 Maya: For the pilot we'll capture metrics: P95 latency, tokens per response, errors per minute, and cost per 1k responses. We'll build dashboards in Console.
00:09:18 (40s) Aaron: Quick demo of Console traces: here you can drill into a request, see token timing, kernel selection, and the autoscaler events. This helps root-cause spikes — e.g., a GPU swap or model fallback.
00:09:45 Carla: Model fallback?
00:09:48 Aaron: If the preferred model hits capacity, Smart Routing may route to a compatible variant (lower precision or smaller family) depending on your fallback policy. You can set per-route fallback thresholds.
00:10:05 Ethan: Does fallback affect logits? Will responses be noticeably different?
00:10:11 Aaron: It can — smaller variants or more quantized runs may change lexical choices slightly. We recommend canary rollouts and quality thresholds; Redwood Optimize can detect regressions against your eval set.
00:10:27 (30s) Maya: We should talk about concurrency and rate limits: default hosted tier has soft limits but you can request increases. For bursts, there's a small queue and you can configure graceful degradation.
00:10:45 Lina: If we use Dedicated, do we still get the Console metrics and the same API?
00:10:52 Aaron: Yes — same Console and API, just different control plane for Private. Dedicated gives you reserved capacity and predictable throughput.
00:11:05 (1m) Aaron: Now a quick Q&A — Ethan asked about live retries with payment flows. Best practice: for idempotent suggestions it's fine to retry; for monetary charge actions isolate the charge step and gate behind a confirmed final response.
00:11:30 Carla: Any compliance certifications for EU data residency?
00:11:36 Maya: We have region options and can pin data region. For full compliance we have Private deployments as well. We'll include region controls in the security doc.
00:11:52 (20s) Aaron: Demonstrating a mid-call reconnect: I close the connection and re-open with resume token — you can see the partial completion appends correctly. There can be a 200-500ms gap on resume depending on the server cold path.
00:12:15 Ethan: Performance test plan — can you outline what you'll run?
00:12:20 Aaron: We'll run a 1-hour test with your prompt set at increasing concurrency: ramp 10->200 concurrent, capture P50/P95/P99, error rates, tokens per response and cost. We'll provide raw logs and Console traces.
00:12:40 Maya: Ok let's cover a few quick edge-case questions from Lina. Lina: how do you handle SSO and audit - are logs exportable to our SIEM?
00:12:50 Aaron: Yes, audit logs can stream to your SIEM via our logging integration or S3 dumps; SAML/SCIM are supported.
00:13:02 Lina: KMS for keys?
00:13:05 Maya: We support customer-managed keys via KMS/HSM in Private and Dedicated and can offer envelope encryption for hosted in some tiers.
00:13:18 (pause)
00:13:30 Aaron: Last demo item — using the API to set model params per-route. You can pin an endpoint to use low-latency profile: model variant, smaller max_length, and prefix cache TTL. These are per-route in Console.
00:13:48 Carla: Great. Can you also show cost impact of increasing temperature?
00:13:53 Aaron: Temperature itself doesn't change tokens; cost is driven by token count and model. However higher temp may produce longer outputs, so indirectly cost can rise.
00:14:08 Maya: Ok we're approaching time. Quick recap and next steps.
00:14:14 Maya: Action items: Maya will send pricing + SLA, Aaron will run the benchmark, Carla will send prompt set. We'll reconvene once the benchmark is done to decide Dedicated vs Hosted pilot.
00:14:29 Lina: Sounds good. Quick note — we'll need security contact details in the doc.
00:14:34 Maya: Will include contact and SOC2 link.
00:14:40 (end)

Notes: Transcription has small errors (SAML as S-A-M-L, SOC2 as SOC two in places), speaker attribution in a few frames may be off.
